name: Learn: Pod & Container Security
description: Harden pods step by step — run as non-root, drop Linux capabilities, read-only root filesystem, seccomp RuntimeDefault, and enforce the restricted Pod Security Standard on a namespace. Exam-focused securityContext and Pod Security Admission practice.
objective: CKS › Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities (20%). Goal: harden workloads — securityContext (runAsNonRoot, drop caps), readOnlyRootFilesystem, seccomp, and Pod Security Admission.

questions.title: Run as non-root (runAsNonRoot + runAsUser)
questions.teach:
By default a container may run as **root (UID 0)** — a big attack surface. The `securityContext` fixes the runtime identity:

- `runAsNonRoot: true` — kubelet **refuses to start** the pod if the image/config would resolve to UID 0 (fails at runtime with `CreateContainerConfigError`, not at admission).
- `runAsUser: <uid>` / `runAsGroup: <gid>` — pin a specific UID/GID. `runAsGroup` is **pod-level** (and container-level); setting a non-zero `runAsUser` alone does **not** satisfy `runAsNonRoot` unless the UID is non-zero.
- `fsGroup: <gid>` — **pod-level only**; owns mounted volumes so a non-root user can write to them.
- `supplementalGroups` — extra GIDs added to the process.

**Pod-level vs container-level:** identical fields can live in `spec.securityContext` (applies to all containers) or `spec.containers[].securityContext`. **Container-level wins** on conflict. Note `fsGroup`/`supplementalGroups` exist only at pod level; `capabilities`/`readOnlyRootFilesystem`/`allowPrivilegeEscalation` only at container level.

**Gotchas:**
- `runAsNonRoot: true` with an image whose `USER` is root (and no `runAsUser`) — pod will NOT start. busybox defaults to root, so you must pin a non-zero `runAsUser`.
- `runAsUser: 0` + `runAsNonRoot: true` = contradiction → pod fails to start.
- The check is on the UID **number**, not a username; the UID need not exist in `/etc/passwd`.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cks-podsec`, create a pod `secure-app` using image `busybox:1.36` running `sleep 3600`, with a container `securityContext` that sets `runAsNonRoot: true` and `runAsUser: 1000`.

Target: pod `secure-app` is Running and its container reports `runAsNonRoot=true` and `runAsUser=1000`.
questions.hint: `kubectl run secure-app -n cks-podsec --image=busybox:1.36 --overrides='{...securityContext...}' -- sleep 3600`, or write a YAML with `spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true` and `runAsUser: 1000` and `kubectl apply -f`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secure-app
  namespace: cks-podsec
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      runAsNonRoot: true
      runAsUser: 1000
YAML
kubectl -n cks-podsec wait --for=condition=Ready pod/secure-app --timeout=60s

verification.description: pod secure-app runs non-root as UID 1000

questions.title: Drop ALL Linux capabilities
questions.teach:
Linux **capabilities** slice up root's powers (e.g. `NET_RAW`, `CHOWN`, `NET_BIND_SERVICE`, `SYS_TIME`). Containers get a default set from the runtime even when non-root. Best practice is to **drop ALL** and add back only what you truly need.

```yaml
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
    add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]
```

**Key facts:**
- `capabilities` is **container-level only** — it has no meaning at `spec.securityContext` (pod level).
- Write names **without the `CAP_` prefix** (`NET_BIND_SERVICE`, not `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`). `kubectl describe` / `getpcaps` show them with the prefix.
- `drop: ["ALL"]` then `add: [...]` is the restricted-standard pattern; the *restricted* PSS additionally **forbids adding anything except `NET_BIND_SERVICE`**.
- Adding capabilities is distinct from `privileged: true`, which grants effectively **all** capabilities plus device access — never combine with hardening.

**Gotchas:**
- Drop and add can both be present; if the same cap is in both, **add wins** (it is granted).
- Dropping a cap an app silently relies on (e.g. `CHOWN`, `SETUID`) causes runtime failures, not a scheduling error.
- A non-root user cannot use most capabilities anyway unless file/ambient capabilities are set — dropping ALL is still the correct hardening.
questions.prompt:
Create a pod `cap-app` in `cks-podsec` (image `busybox:1.36`, `sleep 3600`) that **drops ALL** capabilities and **adds** only `NET_BIND_SERVICE`. Keep it non-root (`runAsUser: 1000`).

Target: pod `cap-app` is Running with `capabilities.drop=[ALL]` and `capabilities.add=[NET_BIND_SERVICE]`.
questions.hint: Add under the container `securityContext`: `capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"], add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"] }`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: cap-app
  namespace: cks-podsec
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      runAsUser: 1000
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
        add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]
YAML
kubectl -n cks-podsec wait --for=condition=Ready pod/cap-app --timeout=60s

verification.description: cap-app drops ALL and adds only NET_BIND_SERVICE

questions.title: Read-only root filesystem
questions.teach:
`readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` makes the container's `/` **immutable** — an attacker can't drop binaries or tamper with files. But many programs need *some* writable path (e.g. `/tmp`, `/var/run`, cache dirs).

The pattern: set the root read-only, then mount a writable volume at just the paths that must be writable.

```yaml
securityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true   # container-level only
volumeMounts:
- {name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}
volumes:
- {name: tmp, emptyDir: {}}
```

**Writable-volume options for scratch space:**
- `emptyDir: {}` — node disk, lives as long as the pod.
- `emptyDir: { medium: Memory, sizeLimit: 64Mi }` — tmpfs (RAM-backed); counts against the container's memory.
- A mounted ConfigMap/Secret is read-only too, so secrets still mount fine with a read-only root.

**Other related container-level toggles (restricted PSS):**
- `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` — stops a process gaining more privileges than its parent (blocks setuid escalation); required by *restricted*.
- `privileged: false` — the default; `true` disables this hardening entirely.

**Gotchas:**
- `readOnlyRootFilesystem` is **container-level only** — no effect under pod `securityContext`.
- Forgetting the writable mount → app crashes when it writes logs/temp files (often a `CrashLoopBackOff`, not an admission error).
- Each writable path needs its own mount; the root stays read-only for everything else.
questions.prompt:
Create a pod `ro-app` in `cks-podsec` (image `busybox:1.36`, `sleep 3600`, `runAsUser: 1000`) with `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, plus an `emptyDir` volume mounted at `/tmp` so it can still run.

Target: pod `ro-app` is Running with `readOnlyRootFilesystem=true` and a volumeMount at `/tmp`.
questions.hint: Container `securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`; add `volumes: [{name: tmp, emptyDir: {}}]` and `volumeMounts: [{name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}]`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: ro-app
  namespace: cks-podsec
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      runAsUser: 1000
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
YAML
kubectl -n cks-podsec wait --for=condition=Ready pod/ro-app --timeout=60s

verification.description: ro-app has read-only root fs + emptyDir at /tmp and is Running

questions.title: seccomp RuntimeDefault
questions.teach:
**seccomp** filters which Linux syscalls a container may make. Kubernetes containers run **Unconfined** by default. The *restricted* Pod Security Standard requires either `RuntimeDefault` or a `Localhost` profile.

**Three `seccompProfile.type` values:**
- `RuntimeDefault` — the container runtime's built-in profile (containerd/CRI-O). No file needed; blocks dangerous syscalls at near-zero cost.
- `Localhost` — a custom profile JSON on the node under the kubelet seccomp root (`/var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/`); **requires** `localhostProfile: <relative/path.json>`.
- `Unconfined` — no filtering (the default); **rejected** by the restricted standard.

```yaml
securityContext:          # pod-level: applies to all containers
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
```

**Pod-level vs container-level:** can live in either `securityContext`; container-level overrides pod-level for that container.

**Gotchas:**
- `type` is **case-sensitive** (`RuntimeDefault`, not `runtimedefault`/`runtimeDefault`).
- `localhostProfile` is valid **only** with `type: Localhost`, and the path is **relative** to the kubelet seccomp dir, not absolute.
- Setting it at pod level alone is enough for the restricted standard; the older annotation `seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/pod` is **deprecated/removed** — use the `seccompProfile` field.
questions.prompt:
Create a pod `seccomp-app` in `cks-podsec` (image `busybox:1.36`, `sleep 3600`, `runAsUser: 1000`) with a `seccompProfile` of type `RuntimeDefault`.

Target: pod `seccomp-app` is Running with `seccompProfile.type=RuntimeDefault`.
questions.hint: Add `seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }` under the pod or container `securityContext`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: seccomp-app
  namespace: cks-podsec
spec:
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      runAsUser: 1000
YAML
kubectl -n cks-podsec wait --for=condition=Ready pod/seccomp-app --timeout=60s

questions.title: Enforce restricted Pod Security Admission
questions.teach:
**Pod Security Admission (PSA)** is a built-in admission controller enforcing the three **Pod Security Standards** per namespace via **labels** — no external webhook.

**Three levels:** `privileged` (no restrictions) → `baseline` (blocks known escalations) → `restricted` (hardened: non-root, drop ALL caps, seccomp, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, no host namespaces).

**Three modes**, each its own label:
- `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=<level>` — **rejects** violating pods at the API server.
- `pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=<level>` — allows, returns a warning to the client.
- `pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=<level>` — allows, records an audit annotation.

**Pin a version** per mode with `pod-security.kubernetes.io/<mode>-version=<v1.xx>` (e.g. `enforce-version=v1.30`) so policy doesn't drift on cluster upgrade; omit it and it means `latest`.

```bash
kubectl label ns cks-locked \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.30 --overwrite
```

**Gotchas:**
- `enforce` only checks pods at **create/update** — it does **not** evict pods already running when the label is added.
- Common safe rollout: set `warn`/`audit` first to preview, then flip `enforce`.
- You can combine modes/levels on one namespace (e.g. `enforce=baseline`, `warn=restricted`).
- Needs `--overwrite` to change an existing label; labels are case-sensitive and the version must be a real `v1.xx` string.
- PSA replaces the removed **PodSecurityPolicy (PSP)**; it works at **namespace** granularity, not per-pod.
questions.prompt:
Label namespace `cks-locked` to **enforce** the `restricted` Pod Security Standard, pinned to version `v1.30`.

Target: namespace `cks-locked` has label `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted` and `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.30`.

verification.description: cks-locked enforces restricted pinned to v1.30
